title: Dispatchable, Firm Power: An Overview
lede: The burner (MetroVolt) is designed to supply power on command, around the clock, independent of weather or time of day.
body: Firm power is capacity a grid operator can count on being there when it is called. Dispatchable power can be raised or lowered on command to follow demand. A resource can be one without the other: a run-of-river hydro plant is firm within limits but not freely dispatchable, while a battery is dispatchable but energy-limited. The burner (MetroVolt) is designed to be both, with output set by fuel and plasma control rather than by sun or wind.

The core is a D-3He tandem-mirror generator with direct energy conversion (DEC). Because charged fusion products are turned into electricity electrostatically instead of boiling water, the machine has no large thermal mass gating how fast it can change output, and no cooling-water draw gating where it can sit. Those two properties are what make the grid-and-cities case distinct from a conventional thermal plant.

Honest framing: this is a design

MetroVolt is at the design-and-simulation stage. A test burner is targeted for around 2032 and a commercial unit around 2036, after the breeder (Hyperion) is built. No hardware net-gain result exists yet. Four physics gates are open and stated plainly across these pages: plug-coil stress, plug operating regime, helium-3 supply, and availability. The firmness described here is an engineering target the design is aimed at, not a measured capability.

The rest of this category walks through what firm power means for renewables integration, baseload, near-demand siting, interconnection, black-start, and resilience, and where each of those runs into the open gates.

title: What Is Firm Power
lede: Firm power is capacity a grid can rely on at the moment of peak need; it is the scarce commodity as variable renewables grow.
body: Reliability at the peak, not on average

Grid operators plan for the worst hour, not the average one. A resource's firm capacity is the fraction of its nameplate rating that can be counted on during that worst hour. Solar has near-zero firm capacity after sunset; wind's firm capacity is a small fraction of nameplate during a still, cold evening. A resource that reliably shows up at the peak carries high capacity value even if its nameplate is modest.

The burner (MetroVolt) is designed as a firm resource: a steady-state D-3He tandem-mirror generator intended to run continuously and to be dispatched up or down within its operating band. In principle its firm capacity is close to its nameplate, limited mainly by planned maintenance and forced-outage rate rather than by weather.

As grids add variable renewables, energy becomes abundant at times and scarce at others. The binding problem shifts from producing enough kilowatt-hours to guaranteeing power in the scarce hours. Firm, dispatchable capacity is what closes that gap without over-building storage for multi-day lulls.

Honest gate: the burner's real firm capacity depends on availability, and the design-stage availability estimate is 0.86 to 0.995, against the 0.99982 that a hyperscale Tier III site expects. That is 30 to 100 times more downtime, so a single unit is not yet a sole firm source; fleet redundancy is part of the answer. See the availability pages.

title: Baseload Versus Firm Capacity
lede: Baseload describes how a plant is run; firm capacity describes what a grid can count on. The burner is designed for both roles.
body: Two words that are often confused

Baseload traditionally means a plant run flat-out around the clock because it is cheap to run and slow to change. Firm capacity is the reliability attribute described elsewhere in this category. Historically the two overlapped, since coal and fission plants were both baseload and firm. On a high-renewables grid they separate: the valuable trait is not running flat all the time but being available and adjustable when needed.

The burner (MetroVolt) can serve as a baseload machine, sitting at high output continuously to anchor a data-center campus or a city district. But its design intent is broader: to move within its operating band so it can also firm a renewable-heavy grid rather than only fill the bottom of the load curve.

A tandem mirror is an inherently steady-state confinement scheme: unlike a pulsed tokamak, it is designed to hold a continuous burn. That makes continuous baseload operation natural and avoids the duty-cycle penalties of pulsed machines. Direct energy conversion likewise runs continuously rather than in thermal cycles.

Continuous operation is a design property being studied in simulation, not a demonstrated one. The open plug-confinement and regime gates (the plug operates 166 to 830 times beyond any existing device) mean sustained steady-state burn has not been post-dicted from experiment. Treat baseload capability as a target of the 2032 test unit, not a present fact.

title: Steady-State Burn And Firmness
lede: A tandem mirror is designed to hold a continuous plasma burn, which is what lets a burner behave as a firm, always-on source.
body: Why steady-state matters for the grid

Firm power requires that the generator can, in principle, run without interruption for long periods. Pulsed fusion concepts must repeatedly re-establish the plasma, which complicates always-on grid service. The tandem-mirror architecture is open-ended and magnetostatic: end plugs and a central cell hold a continuous burn rather than a repeated pulse, which is the natural basis for firm output.

The burner's plug fields are extreme by design: 26.49 T at the plug and 17 T at the throat. Those fields set up the axial potential that confines central-cell ions long enough to burn. If sustained, that confinement supports continuous operation; the direct-conversion stage then draws charged-particle power off continuously.

Two of the four honest gates bear directly on steady-state claims. The plug coil is overstressed roughly 3 to 3.9 times at the design bore, so as specified it is not yet buildable. And the plug operating regime sits 166 to 830 times beyond any device operated to date, so continuous confinement cannot be post-dicted from existing data.

The consequence for firmness is honest: steady-state, always-on operation is the design goal that makes MetroVolt attractive for grids and cities, but it is exactly the property the open gates put in question. The 2032 test unit exists to probe whether the burn can be held.
Design-and-simulation finding, not a built-hardware result.

title: Capacity Factor And Availability
lede: Capacity factor is how much energy a plant actually delivers; availability is how often it can. For firm service, availability is the harder target.
body: Capacity factor is annual energy delivered divided by energy at full nameplate. Availability is the fraction of time the plant is able to run when called, whether or not it is dispatched. A peaker can have low capacity factor but high availability. For a firm baseload burner the two are close, because the design intent is to run near full output whenever it is available.

The burner (MetroVolt) targets high capacity factor by running steady-state. The limiting term is availability: forced outages, planned maintenance, and any trip of the plasma or the direct-conversion train subtract from it.

This is the load-bearing grid gate. The design-stage availability estimate is 0.86 to 0.995. A hyperscale Tier III data center expects 0.99982. That is 30 to 100 times more downtime than the most demanding load will tolerate from a single source. It does not sink the case, but it defines it: MetroVolt is not, today, a sole Tier III source, and the design must lean on redundancy, fleet operation, and a grid tie.
Closing this gap is an explicit objective of the test program. Until measured on hardware, treat the numbers above as targets from simulation and reliability modeling.

title: Load Following With A Burner
lede: Dispatchable service means moving output up and down on command; the burner's ramp is limited by plasma control rather than by boiler thermal inertia.
body: Load following is the ability to change output to track demand minute by minute. Steam plants ramp slowly because large metal masses and boilers cannot heat and cool quickly without fatigue. The burner (MetroVolt) has no steam cycle: direct energy conversion turns charged particles into electricity with little thermal mass in the conversion path, so in principle the electrical output can be trimmed by adjusting fuelling and plasma parameters.

Design-stage control levers include fuelling rate, heating power to the plug and central cell, and the bias on the DEC collector stages. Each changes the balance between fusion power produced and power extracted. The control problem is coupling these without disturbing confinement.

Fast load following is a design aspiration, not a demonstrated ramp rate. Because the plug regime is 166 to 830 times beyond experiment, the true stable operating band, and how quickly output can be moved within it without losing the burn, are open questions. Deep, fast turndown may trade against confinement margin.

Honest position: MetroVolt is designed to be dispatchable, and DEC removes the thermal-inertia limit that slows steam plants. Whether the plasma will tolerate rapid, repeated dispatch is exactly what the 2032 test unit must show.

title: Grid Firming Alongside Renewables
lede: A firm, dispatchable burner is a complement to wind and solar, filling the hours and seasons when variable output falls short.
body: On a decarbonizing grid, the cheapest energy increasingly comes from wind and solar, but their output is variable and occasionally absent for days. The role of a firm resource is to guarantee power in those hours without building storage for every rare multi-day lull. The burner (MetroVolt) is positioned as that firming partner, not as a replacement for renewables.

Because it is dispatchable, a burner can sit back when renewables are plentiful and ramp when they fade, improving the utilization of the whole system. Its firm capacity is what lets an operator retire fossil peakers while keeping resource adequacy.

To firm renewables well, a resource must be (1) reliably available at the peak, (2) able to ramp, and (3) sited where the grid needs it. MetroVolt's design targets all three, but each meets an open gate: availability (0.86 to 0.995 vs 0.99982 Tier III), unproven ramp under a plug regime far beyond experiment, and siting that still depends on interconnection approval.

This is a design-stage complementarity argument. No burner has firmed a real grid. The claim is that the architecture, low-neutron D-3He with direct conversion and near-zero water, is well matched to the firming role once the physics gates are closed after the ~2032 test unit.

title: Why Renewables Need Firm Partners
lede: Variable renewables reduce fuel burn but do not by themselves guarantee power at the worst hour; firm capacity closes the reliability gap.
body: A grid can be 80 percent renewable in energy terms and still fail in the scarce hours if it lacks firm capacity. The gap appears on calm, cloudy winter evenings when demand is high and both wind and solar are low. Storage helps for hours; it becomes impractical to size for the rare multi-day event. That residual is what firm resources fill.

Firm partners let operators build fewer redundant renewables and less long-duration storage while still meeting reliability standards. The burner (MetroVolt) is designed to be one such partner, running steady and dispatching when the variable fleet cannot.

A firm partner should be low-carbon, sitable near load, and water-light so it can be added where renewables and transmission are already stretched. MetroVolt's D-3He core is low-neutron (5.44 percent of power in neutrons, not aneutronic) and its DEC design needs almost no cooling water, which suits constrained urban and arid sites.

The firm-partner role assumes the machine achieves the availability and dispatch it targets. Today those are open: availability is estimated at 0.86 to 0.995 versus 0.99982 for Tier III, and the plug physics is far beyond any tested device. The value proposition is real only after the gates close.

title: The Duck Curve And Firm Power
lede: Midday solar carves a deep belly into net load and a steep evening ramp; firm dispatchable generation is what climbs that ramp.
body: When abundant solar is added, the net load, demand minus renewables, sags at midday and rises sharply as the sun sets while people come home. Plotted over a day the shape resembles a duck. Two features stress the grid: the deep midday belly, where inflexible plants must back down, and the steep evening neck, where several gigawatts must appear within a couple of hours.

A firm, flexible resource is valuable on both counts. It can reduce output during the belly and ramp hard up the neck. The burner (MetroVolt), designed to be dispatchable without steam-cycle inertia, is aimed at exactly this ramp.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 258" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="258" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">The evening ramp</text><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="600" y2="200" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="60" y1="60" x2="60" y2="200" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="330" y="230" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">hour of day</text><text x="30" y="130" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39" transform="rotate(-90 30 130)">demand</text><path d="M60,110 C160,90 220,180 330,185 C440,180 520,80 600,70" fill="none" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M60,200 L60,150 L600,150 L600,200 Z" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.35"/><text x="500" y="175" font-size="11" fill="#232C39">firm generation</text><text x="360" y="95" font-size="11" fill="#232C39">net load</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Deep midday belly, steep evening neck; firm generation must climb it.</text></svg>

The neck of the duck grows steeper as solar penetration rises. Meeting it requires resources that can move quickly and reliably. DEC removes the thermal-mass limit that slows steam plants, which is the design basis for a fast burner ramp.

MetroVolt's ramp capability is a simulated design target, not a measured one. The stable operating band and achievable ramp rate depend on plug physics that sits 166 to 830 times beyond any operated device. The duck-curve fit is a motivating use case, contingent on the test program.

title: Seasonal And Multi-Day Lulls
lede: Wind and solar droughts can last days or align with seasonal demand peaks; firm generation covers the gaps storage cannot economically span.
body: Batteries excel at shifting energy across hours. They are poorly suited to a week of low wind in midwinter, because the stored energy required grows with the duration of the lull. These Dunkelflaute events, dark and windless spells, are rare but decisive for reliability planning. A grid must cover them or accept blackouts.

Firm generation, run continuously or dispatched through the lull, is the practical answer. The burner (MetroVolt) is designed to run steady-state indefinitely on stored D-3He fuel, independent of weather, which is the property a multi-day lull demands.

Because fusion fuel is energy-dense, a burner can hold long-duration firmness without a large fuel yard. But this is where the third honest gate bites: helium-3 demand for a commercial unit is roughly 400 times domestic supply. Multi-day firmness assumes a fuel supply that does not yet exist at terrestrial scale, which is why the breeder-bred He-3 pathway and lunar He-3 matter.
Honest summary: the architecture is well matched to seasonal firmness, but the fuel-supply gate must be closed before a fleet can deliver it.

title: The Capacity Value Of Firm Generation
lede: Capacity value measures how much a resource contributes to meeting the peak; firm generation typically carries the highest value per megawatt.
body: Planners assign each resource a capacity credit, or effective load-carrying capability, that reflects how much it reduces the risk of shortfall at peak. A resource that is reliably present when the system is tight earns close to its full nameplate; a weather-dependent one earns a fraction. Firm dispatchable plants therefore anchor resource-adequacy plans.

The burner (MetroVolt) is designed to earn high capacity credit because it is not weather-dependent. Its credit is set instead by its forced-outage rate and maintenance schedule, the same terms that govern any thermal or nuclear unit.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 250" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="250" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Illustrative capacity credit as % of nameplate</text><text x="240" y="74" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Solar</text><rect x="250" y="56" width="34" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="292" y="74" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">10%</text><text x="240" y="114" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Wind</text><rect x="250" y="96" width="68" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="326" y="114" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">20%</text><text x="240" y="154" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">4 h battery</text><rect x="250" y="136" width="170" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="428" y="154" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">50%</text><text x="240" y="194" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Firm burner (target)</text><rect x="250" y="176" width="306" height="26" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="564" y="194" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">90%</text><text x="24" y="238" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Firm resources concentrate value at the peak.</text></svg>

A resource cannot earn credit it is not available to deliver. The design-stage availability of 0.86 to 0.995 means MetroVolt's capacity credit, while high relative to variable resources, is capped below what a Tier III load expects from a single source (0.99982). Fleet redundancy raises the effective credit above any one unit.
These capacity-value comparisons are qualitative and design-stage. They describe the role the architecture is designed to play, not a validated grid result.

title: Dispatchability Versus Intermittency
lede: Intermittent resources produce on nature's schedule; dispatchable resources produce on the operator's. A grid needs enough of the latter.
body: Intermittent generation, wind and solar, produces when the resource is available. Dispatchable generation produces when instructed, up to its rating. Most grids blend both: cheap intermittent energy plus enough dispatchable capacity to keep supply matched to demand every second. The mix determines reliability.

The burner (MetroVolt) is designed as a dispatchable resource. Its fuel is stored, its confinement is steady-state, and its direct-conversion output can, in principle, be trimmed on command. That places it firmly on the dispatchable end, alongside gas and nuclear but without their water footprint or carbon.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Dispatch on command</text><rect x="55" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="113" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Operator</text><text x="113" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">dispatch signal</text><line x1="171" y1="143" x2="187" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="187,138 193,143 187,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="193" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="251" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Plasma</text><text x="251" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">control</text><line x1="309" y1="143" x2="325" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,138 331,143 325,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="389" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">DEC</text><text x="389" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">output set</text><line x1="447" y1="143" x2="463" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="463,138 469,143 463,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="469" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="527" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Grid</text><text x="527" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">matched</text></svg>

As intermittent share rises, each remaining dispatchable megawatt becomes more valuable because it must cover a larger and more variable residual. Under-provisioning dispatchable capacity risks shortfalls; over-provisioning wastes capital. A water-light, sitable dispatchable resource widens where that capacity can be placed.

Dispatchability here is a design property. The achievable dispatch band and ramp are unproven because the plug regime is far beyond any operated device, and single-unit availability (0.86 to 0.995) trails Tier III (0.99982). MetroVolt is a candidate dispatchable resource pending its 2032 test.

title: Pairing Firm Generation With Storage
lede: Batteries and a firm burner are complements: storage handles fast, short swings while firm generation carries sustained and multi-day load.
body: Storage and firm generation solve different problems. Batteries respond in milliseconds and are ideal for smoothing second-to-minute variability, providing fast frequency response, and shifting a few hours of energy. They are poorly suited to sustained output over days. Firm generation carries the sustained and multi-day load but responds more slowly than a battery.

Pairing the two gives a campus or microgrid the best of both: a battery covers the instant a fault occurs and the fast transients, while the burner (MetroVolt) provides the underlying firm energy. This pairing also eases the burner's ramp duty.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Storage plus firm generation</text><rect x="55" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="113" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Battery</text><text x="113" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">fast transient</text><line x1="171" y1="143" x2="187" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="187,138 193,143 187,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="193" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="251" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Burner</text><text x="251" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">sustained firm</text><line x1="309" y1="143" x2="325" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,138 331,143 325,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="389" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Controller</text><text x="389" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">blends</text><line x1="447" y1="143" x2="463" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="463,138 469,143 463,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="469" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="527" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Load</text><text x="527" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">served</text></svg>
Why the pairing helps the gates

Storage can partially buffer the availability gate. If a burner unit trips, a co-sited battery can bridge seconds to minutes while a backup unit or the grid picks up load, softening the impact of the 0.86 to 0.995 availability against a 0.99982 Tier III expectation. Storage does not close the gate but it reduces the consequence of a single forced outage.
This is an architecture-level design argument. The burner is not built; the pairing is a way the design intends to reach data-center-grade continuity given the open availability gate.

title: Reserve Margins And Adequacy
lede: Reserve margin is the cushion of firm capacity above peak demand; firm dispatchable resources are what fill it as fossil plants retire.
body: A grid keeps a reserve margin, firm capacity above forecast peak demand, so it can absorb an unexpected outage, a demand spike, or a forecast error. Typical target margins are on the order of a tenth to a fifth above peak. The margin must be met with resources that count at the peak, which is capacity value, not average energy.

As coal and older gas retire, the firm capacity that filled reserve margins leaves the system. Replacing it with variable renewables alone erodes the margin, because their capacity credit is low. Firm dispatchable additions like the burner (MetroVolt) are designed to backfill this reserve.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="170" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Reserve margin above peak</text><text x="240" y="74" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Peak demand</text><rect x="250" y="56" width="283" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="541" y="74" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">100%</text><text x="240" y="114" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Firm capacity needed</text><rect x="250" y="96" width="326" height="26" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="584" y="114" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">115%</text><text x="24" y="158" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Firm capacity must exceed peak by a planning margin.</text></svg>
Firmness, not energy, fills the margin

A megawatt-hour of surplus solar at noon does nothing for a reserve margin measured at the winter evening peak. Only firm capacity that is available at that peak contributes. This is the crux of why grids adding renewables still procure firm resources.

MetroVolt's contribution to a reserve margin equals its firm capacity, which is limited by its availability (0.86 to 0.995, design-stage) and best realized across a redundant fleet rather than a single unit. The contribution is real in principle and unproven in hardware.

title: Resource Adequacy Basics
lede: Resource adequacy is the assurance that enough firm capacity exists to meet demand in all but the rarest hours; firm generators are its backbone.
body: Resource adequacy is measured with metrics like loss-of-load expectation, the expected number of hours per year that demand exceeds available supply. Planners size the fleet so that number stays below a small target, often a fraction of a day per decade. Meeting it requires firm capacity that is present during the tightest hours.

Firm dispatchable resources dominate adequacy planning because their contribution is predictable. Variable resources contribute in proportion to their capacity credit, which falls as more of them are added and their output correlates. The burner (MetroVolt) is designed to add high, weather-independent adequacy.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 256" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="256" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">What resource adequacy requires</text><rect x="40" y="56" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="56" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="78" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Firm capacity available at the tightest hours</text><rect x="40" y="100" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="100" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="122" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Predictable contribution, low correlation with weather</text><rect x="40" y="144" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="144" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="166" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Redundancy so one outage does not cause shortfall</text><rect x="40" y="188" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="188" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="210" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Fuel available for sustained and multi-day events</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">MetroVolt is designed against these four requirements.</text></svg>
Where the burner helps and where it does not yet

MetroVolt's weather independence and steady-state design suit adequacy planning. Two gates limit today's contribution: availability (0.86 to 0.995 vs 0.99982 Tier III) constrains single-unit reliability, and He-3 fuel demand roughly 400 times domestic supply constrains how large a fleet can actually be fuelled without the breeder-bred and lunar pathways.
Honest position: the architecture is a strong adequacy candidate on paper, contingent on closing the availability and fuel gates after the ~2032 test unit.

title: Near-Demand Siting: An Overview
lede: Placing generation next to the load it serves shortens transmission, reduces losses, and can relieve congested corridors.
body: Bringing the plant to the load

Most large power plants sit far from cities because they need cooling water, fuel logistics, or buffer land. That distance requires long, high-voltage transmission, which incurs losses, congestion, and long build times. Placing firm generation near the load, at the edge of a city or beside a data-center campus, avoids much of that.

The burner (MetroVolt) is designed for near-demand siting. Direct energy conversion removes the steam cycle and its cooling-water draw, so the machine does not need a river or coastline. Its low-neutron D-3He core reduces shielding mass relative to a D-T plant. Together these shrink the footprint and loosen the siting constraint.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 258" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="258" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Generation at the edge of the load</text><rect x="360" y="90" width="220" height="120" rx="8" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="470" y="80" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Load center</text><rect x="375" y="150" width="26" height="60" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="415" y="120" width="26" height="90" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="455" y="160" width="26" height="50" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="495" y="130" width="26" height="80" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="535" y="145" width="26" height="65" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="70" y="120" width="150" height="70" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="70" y="120" width="150" height="8" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="145" y="150" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">MetroVolt</text><text x="145" y="168" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">unit</text><line x1="220" y1="155" x2="360" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="3"/><text x="290" y="140" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">short interconnect</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">A short interconnect replaces a long transmission corridor.</text></svg>

Siting near load reduces line losses, defers or avoids new transmission, improves local voltage support, and can provide black-start and islanding value to the community it sits in. For a data center it means firm power behind or beside the meter rather than hundreds of kilometres away.

Near-demand siting still requires interconnection approval, community acceptance, and a safety case for an urban-adjacent nuclear facility. And the availability gate (0.86 to 0.995 vs 0.99982) means a near-sited unit still needs a grid tie or redundancy; proximity does not by itself make a single unit Tier III firm.

title: Relieving Transmission Congestion
lede: Congested corridors cap how much power can reach a load; firm generation sited behind the constraint delivers power the wires cannot.
body: When the wires are the bottleneck

Transmission congestion occurs when the demand to move power across a corridor exceeds the corridor's rating. The grid then dispatches more expensive local generation or curtails cheaper remote generation, and reliability margins shrink downstream of the constraint. Building new lines takes many years and faces siting opposition.

Generation placed on the load side of a constraint delivers power that never has to cross the congested wires. The burner (MetroVolt), being water-light and compact, can be sited inside constrained load pockets where a conventional thermal plant could not, directly relieving the corridor.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 258" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="258" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Local generation behind the constraint</text><rect x="360" y="90" width="220" height="120" rx="8" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="470" y="80" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Load center</text><rect x="375" y="150" width="26" height="60" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="415" y="120" width="26" height="90" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="455" y="160" width="26" height="50" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="495" y="130" width="26" height="80" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="535" y="145" width="26" height="65" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="70" y="120" width="150" height="70" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="70" y="120" width="150" height="8" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="145" y="150" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">MetroVolt</text><text x="145" y="168" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">unit</text><line x1="220" y1="155" x2="360" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="3"/><text x="290" y="140" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">short interconnect</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Firm output inside the load pocket bypasses the congested corridor.</text></svg>

Because MetroVolt can be placed precisely where the grid is tight, it acts as a surgical fix for congestion rather than a bulk energy addition far away. This is especially relevant for fast-growing data-center clusters that overwhelm local transmission faster than new lines can be built.

Relieving congestion is a siting argument, not a claim about the physics being solved. The unit still faces the plug-stress, plug-regime, He-3 supply, and availability gates. Congestion relief is a benefit of where the design can sit, contingent on the machine working, which the 2032 test must show.
related: Relieving The Grid For Data Centers

title: Transmission Deferral
lede: A firm generator sited at a load pocket can defer or avoid new transmission lines that would otherwise take years to permit and build.
body: When demand grows in a location, the default response is to build more transmission to import power. Those projects are slow and contested. A firm generator placed at the load can meet the growth locally, deferring or removing the need for the new line. Utilities value this as non-wires alternative capacity.

The burner (MetroVolt) is designed to be sitable at the load precisely because it does not need cooling water or a large buffer. That makes it a candidate non-wires alternative for load pockets where transmission is the binding constraint, such as dense urban infill or a new compute campus.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Non-wires alternative</text><rect x="55" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="113" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Load</text><text x="113" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">grows</text><line x1="171" y1="143" x2="187" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="187,138 193,143 187,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="193" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="251" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Option A</text><text x="251" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">new line (slow)</text><line x1="309" y1="143" x2="325" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,138 331,143 325,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="389" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Option B</text><text x="389" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">local firm gen</text><line x1="447" y1="143" x2="463" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="463,138 469,143 463,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="469" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="527" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Deferral</text><text x="527" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">achieved</text></svg>

Deferral value depends on being able to add capacity in increments that track demand. MetroVolt's modular unit design supports adding firm capacity in steps at the load, rather than committing to one large remote plant plus its transmission.

Transmission deferral is a system-planning benefit of a working, sitable firm unit. It is contingent on the design closing its physics gates and on a construction timeline: the commercial unit is targeted around 2036, after the ~2032 test. Until then this is a planning argument, not an available option.

title: Urban And Near-City Siting
lede: A water-light, compact burner can sit at the urban edge, close to demand, where conventional thermal plants cannot easily be placed.
body: Why cities are hard for thermal plants

Conventional thermal plants are pushed away from cities by their cooling-water demand, their footprint, and public opposition to smokestacks. Urban and near-city sites are therefore served by long transmission from distant generation. Any firm resource that could sit at the urban edge would shorten that path.

The burner (MetroVolt) is designed for near-city siting. Direct energy conversion removes the steam cycle, so there is no evaporative cooling draw and no cooling tower plume. The low-neutron D-3He core reduces activation and shielding relative to D-T. The footprint is compact and modular. These properties are what make an urban-edge site plausible.

What still governs an urban site

Even a clean, water-light machine must satisfy a nuclear safety case, emergency planning, community consent, and zoning. MetroVolt is low-neutron, not aneutronic, so neutron shielding and activated-material handling are part of the design. Public engagement and licensing are on the critical path for any urban-adjacent site.

Near-city siting is a design goal enabled by the water and footprint advantages, not a permission already granted. It also does not exempt the unit from the availability gate: a near-city unit still needs redundancy or a grid tie to reach data-center-grade firmness.

title: Siting Footprint For Cities
lede: Removing the steam cycle and cooling infrastructure shrinks the plant footprint, which is decisive for siting near dense demand.
body: What takes up space in a power plant

In a conventional thermal plant, a large share of the site is not the reactor or turbine but the heat-rejection system: cooling towers, condensers, intake and outfall structures, and water treatment. Fuel handling and buffer land add more. This is why thermal plants sprawl and why they are hard to fit near a city.

The burner (MetroVolt) replaces the steam cycle with direct energy conversion, eliminating the condenser and the large cooling-water plant. The confinement machine and the DEC train are the core equipment. The result is a materially smaller footprint for a given firm output, which is what a constrained urban-edge parcel requires.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="170" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Illustrative relative site footprint</text><text x="240" y="74" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Thermal plant (with cooling)</text><rect x="250" y="56" width="340" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="598" y="74" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">100</text><text x="240" y="114" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Burner (DEC, water-light)</text><rect x="250" y="96" width="153" height="26" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="411" y="114" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">45</text><text x="24" y="158" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Schematic; removing heat-rejection plant shrinks the site.</text></svg>

MetroVolt is designed in units, so capacity can be matched to a parcel and to demand growth rather than requiring one large footprint up front. Modular units also support phased construction on a constrained site.

Footprint estimates are design-stage and depend on the final shielding and balance-of-plant design; the machine is low-neutron, not aneutronic, so neutron shielding still contributes mass and space. The footprint advantage is real in principle but not yet fixed by a built plant.

title: Brownfield And Repowering Sites
lede: Retiring fossil plants leave behind interconnections and land; a firm burner can reuse that infrastructure to speed near-demand deployment.
body: A retiring coal or gas plant leaves a valuable asset: an existing grid interconnection sized for large firm output, plus permitted industrial land, roads, and often a trained workforce. Reusing these brownfield sites for new firm generation avoids the slowest parts of a greenfield project, chiefly interconnection queues and land acquisition.

The burner (MetroVolt) is a candidate for repowering such sites. Its firm, dispatchable output can inherit the retiring plant's interconnection, while its water-light DEC design frees it from the water rights the old plant depended on, which can be relinquished or repurposed.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Repowering a brownfield site</text><rect x="55" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="113" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Retiring</text><text x="113" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">fossil plant</text><line x1="171" y1="143" x2="187" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="187,138 193,143 187,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="193" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="251" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Keep</text><text x="251" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">interconnect</text><line x1="309" y1="143" x2="325" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,138 331,143 325,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="389" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Install</text><text x="389" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">burner unit</text><line x1="447" y1="143" x2="463" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="463,138 469,143 463,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="469" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="527" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Firm</text><text x="527" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">reconnected</text></svg>

Fossil plants were sited near load and given strong grid ties precisely because they were firm. A firm replacement preserves that grid role, unlike a variable resource that would leave the interconnection underused at the peak. The result maintains local reliability while removing combustion and its water draw.

Repowering is a deployment strategy, not a solved machine. The unit still faces the four physics gates and the ~2032/2036 timeline. Reusing an interconnection also requires studies to confirm the new unit's characteristics match the point of connection.

title: Grid Interconnection: An Overview
lede: Connecting any new generator to the grid requires studies, upgrades, and agreements that govern how the unit behaves at its point of connection.
body: Interconnection is the process of physically and legally connecting a generator to the transmission or distribution system. It involves feasibility and impact studies, identification of any network upgrades, and an interconnection agreement specifying voltage level, protection, and performance requirements. It is often the longest single step in bringing new capacity online.

The burner (MetroVolt) connects through power electronics, since direct energy conversion produces a DC-like output that is inverted to grid-frequency AC. That connection must meet the same grid-code obligations as any generator: voltage and frequency ride-through, reactive support, and protection coordination.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">From DEC output to the grid</text><rect x="55" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="113" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">DEC</text><text x="113" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">output</text><line x1="171" y1="143" x2="187" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="187,138 193,143 187,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="193" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="251" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Power</text><text x="251" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">electronics</text><line x1="309" y1="143" x2="325" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,138 331,143 325,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="389" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Point of</text><text x="389" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">interconnect</text><line x1="447" y1="143" x2="463" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="463,138 469,143 463,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="469" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="527" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Grid</text><text x="527" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">synchronised</text></svg>

Firm, sitable resources have an interconnection advantage when they can reuse an existing point of connection (see brownfield repowering) or site inside a load pocket, avoiding the largest network upgrades. Placing generation at the load can reduce the upgrades the interconnection study would otherwise require.

Interconnection is a real-world process independent of the physics gates, but it presumes a working unit with defined electrical characteristics. Because MetroVolt is at the design stage, its final grid-interface parameters are not yet fixed; interconnection planning is illustrative until the design is built and characterized.

title: Interconnection Queue Challenges
lede: Long interconnection queues delay new capacity; near-demand siting and reused points of connection are ways firm resources can shorten the path.
body: Interconnection queues have grown because far more projects apply than are built, and each application triggers studies whose results depend on every other project in the queue. Network upgrades identified for remote generation, especially large transmission additions, drive multi-year timelines and can cause projects to drop out, restarting the studies for those behind them.

A firm resource sited at the load can sidestep much of this. If it serves demand locally, it may require smaller network upgrades than a remote plant that must export across the system. Reusing a retiring plant's interconnection avoids the queue for a new large tie altogether.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 256" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="256" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Ways to shorten the interconnection path</text><rect x="40" y="56" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="56" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="78" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Site inside the load pocket, minimizing export upgrades</text><rect x="40" y="100" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="100" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="122" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Reuse a retiring fossil plant's existing interconnection</text><rect x="40" y="144" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="144" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="166" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Match unit size to the point-of-connection rating</text><rect x="40" y="188" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="188" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="210" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Provide voltage and frequency support to ease study findings</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Design strategies, not guarantees of a fast queue.</text></svg>

For a data center, connecting the burner (MetroVolt) behind the customer's meter, primarily serving the on-site load, can further reduce interconnection scope compared with a front-of-meter generator exporting to the grid, though grid rules on stand-by and export still apply.

These are strategies to reduce interconnection burden, not proof of speed. They apply to a working unit; MetroVolt is design-stage, with a commercial target around 2036. Queue reform is also a policy matter outside the machine's control.

title: Point Of Interconnection And Voltage Levels
lede: Where and at what voltage a generator connects shapes its cost, its grid role, and the studies it must pass.
body: A generator can connect at distribution voltage, close to end users, or at transmission voltage, into the bulk system. The choice depends on the unit's size and its intended role. Larger firm units connect at higher voltage to move bulk power; units serving a local pocket may connect at distribution level, closer to the load.

The burner (MetroVolt) is designed to be flexible on this point because its output is conditioned by power electronics rather than a fixed synchronous machine. The inverter stage can be configured for the required voltage level and grid-code obligations at the chosen point of interconnection.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Matching the connection voltage</text><rect x="55" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="113" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">DEC</text><text x="113" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">DC-like</text><line x1="171" y1="143" x2="187" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="187,138 193,143 187,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="193" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="251" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Inverter</text><text x="251" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">AC</text><line x1="309" y1="143" x2="325" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,138 331,143 325,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="389" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Step-up</text><text x="389" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">transformer</text><line x1="447" y1="143" x2="463" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="463,138 469,143 463,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="469" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="527" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Grid</text><text x="527" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">MV or HV</text></svg>

A higher-voltage transmission connection reaches more of the system and supports larger export but requires more substation equipment and heavier interconnection studies. A distribution connection is simpler and better suited to serving a co-sited load such as a data center, but limits export and the size of unit that can connect.

Voltage-level choices are project-specific and presume a defined unit. MetroVolt's final ratings are not fixed at the design stage, so the connection options here are illustrative of the flexibility the power-electronics interface is intended to provide.

title: Grid-Code Compliance
lede: Every generator must meet a grid code governing ride-through, reactive support, and protection; the burner meets it through its power-electronics interface.
body: A grid code is the set of technical requirements a generator must meet to connect and operate: staying online through voltage and frequency disturbances (ride-through), supplying or absorbing reactive power for voltage control, limiting harmonics, and coordinating protection so faults are cleared cleanly. Compliance is mandatory and tested before commissioning.

The burner (MetroVolt) interfaces through inverters, so much of its grid-code behaviour is set in the power-electronics control rather than in machine physics. Modern grid-forming and grid-following inverter controls can meet ride-through, reactive-power, and harmonic requirements, which is the basis for MetroVolt's compliance design.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 256" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="256" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Core grid-code obligations</text><rect x="40" y="56" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="56" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="78" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Fault ride-through: stay connected through voltage dips</text><rect x="40" y="100" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="100" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="122" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Frequency response: adjust output as frequency deviates</text><rect x="40" y="144" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="144" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="166" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Reactive power: support local voltage within a range</text><rect x="40" y="188" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="188" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="210" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Protection and harmonics: clear faults, keep clean waveform</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Delivered largely through inverter control design.</text></svg>

The power-electronics interface gives fine control over grid-code behaviour, and can provide services a synchronous machine cannot, such as fast, programmable reactive support. But inverter-based resources must be designed carefully to provide adequate fault current and stable behaviour on weak grids, which is an active engineering area.

Grid-code compliance is a design and testing task that applies once the unit exists. MetroVolt's inverter design is at the concept stage; compliance is a target of the engineering program, verified only on built hardware.

title: Synchronous Versus Inverter-Based Connection
lede: Traditional plants connect through spinning synchronous machines; the burner connects through inverters, which changes how it supports the grid.
body: A conventional thermal or hydro plant connects through a large spinning generator synchronized to grid frequency. Its rotating mass provides inertia that resists frequency change and supplies large fault current naturally. An inverter-based resource connects through power electronics that convert DC-like power to AC; it has no inherent rotating mass and must provide grid services through control.

The burner (MetroVolt) is inverter-based because direct energy conversion yields a DC-like output. This is a fundamental difference from a steam plant and shapes the grid services it can and cannot provide natively.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Inverter-based grid support</text><rect x="55" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="113" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">DEC</text><text x="113" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">DC-like</text><line x1="171" y1="143" x2="187" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="187,138 193,143 187,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="193" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="251" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Inverter</text><text x="251" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">control</text><line x1="309" y1="143" x2="325" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,138 331,143 325,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="389" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Synthetic</text><text x="389" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">inertia + Q</text><line x1="447" y1="143" x2="463" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="463,138 469,143 463,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="469" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="527" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Grid</text><text x="527" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">support</text></svg>

An inverter-based unit does not supply physical inertia unless its controls emulate it (synthetic inertia), and it must be engineered to deliver adequate fault current and to remain stable on weak grids. In exchange it offers fast, precise, programmable control of active and reactive power that synchronous machines cannot match.

As grids shift toward inverter-based resources overall, the burner fits that direction but inherits its challenges. MetroVolt's inverter behaviour, including synthetic inertia and fault-current capability, is a design objective not yet demonstrated on hardware.

title: Grid-Forming Inverters And DEC
lede: Grid-forming inverters can set voltage and frequency rather than follow them, letting an inverter-based burner help anchor a weak or islanded grid.
body: A grid-following inverter measures the grid's voltage and frequency and injects current in step with them; it needs a grid already there to synchronize to. A grid-forming inverter instead sets its own voltage and frequency reference, behaving like a voltage source. Grid-forming control can start and stabilize a grid, ride through disturbances more robustly, and support weak grids.

Because the burner (MetroVolt) connects through power electronics fed by direct energy conversion, it can in principle use grid-forming control. That capability underpins black-start and islanding value: a grid-forming unit can energize a dead network and hold a microgrid together.

Why it matters for cities and campuses

A near-demand burner using grid-forming inverters could provide local voltage and frequency support, help restart a section of grid after an outage, and run a campus microgrid in island mode. These are services increasingly scarce as spinning machines retire.

Grid-forming operation is a control-design capability, credible for inverter-based resources but unproven for MetroVolt specifically. It also depends on adequate energy behind the inverter, which brings back the availability and steady-burn gates. Treat it as a design objective.

title: Reactive Power And Voltage Support
lede: Grids need reactive power to hold voltage; an inverter-based burner can supply or absorb it on command, aiding local voltage stability.
body: Alternating-current grids carry both real power, which does work, and reactive power, which sustains the voltage that lets real power flow. Loads, lines, and transformers consume reactive power, and without local sources voltage sags, especially at the ends of long feeders and in dense load pockets. Utilities install capacitors and specialized equipment to supply it.

An inverter-based generator can supply or absorb reactive power directly by adjusting its control, independent of its real-power output. The burner (MetroVolt), connected through inverters, can therefore act as a local voltage-support resource in addition to supplying firm real power.

A unit sited inside a load pocket provides voltage support exactly where it is needed, reducing the need for separate reactive equipment and improving the stability of the local grid. This is one of the ancillary services that make near-demand siting valuable beyond energy alone.

Reactive-power capability follows from the inverter interface and is standard for inverter-based resources, but MetroVolt's specific ratings are design-stage. Reactive support also requires the unit to be online, which returns to the availability gate.

title: Frequency Response And Inertia
lede: Grid frequency reflects the instant balance of supply and demand; firm resources with fast response help keep it within limits.
body: Grid frequency, nominally 50 or 60 Hz, rises when generation exceeds load and falls when load exceeds generation. Large spinning machines store kinetic energy that slows frequency change, buying seconds for controls to respond; this is inertia. After the initial dip, primary frequency response adjusts generator output to arrest and correct the deviation.

As inverter-based resources replace spinning plants, physical inertia declines and frequency can move faster after a disturbance. Fast-responding resources become more valuable. An inverter-based burner can provide programmable frequency response and, through controls, synthetic inertia.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 258" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="258" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Frequency after a generation loss</text><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="600" y2="200" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="60" y1="60" x2="60" y2="200" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="330" y="230" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">hour of day</text><text x="30" y="130" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39" transform="rotate(-90 30 130)">demand</text><path d="M60,110 C160,90 220,180 330,185 C440,180 520,80 600,70" fill="none" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M60,200 L60,150 L600,150 L600,200 Z" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.35"/><text x="500" y="175" font-size="11" fill="#232C39">firm generation</text><text x="360" y="95" font-size="11" fill="#232C39">net load</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Inertia slows the dip; primary response arrests and restores frequency.</text></svg>

The burner (MetroVolt) can be programmed to change output in response to frequency deviations and, with grid-forming control, to emulate inertia by injecting power in the first instants of a disturbance. Paired with a co-sited battery, the fastest response can come from storage while the burner provides sustained correction.

Frequency response and synthetic inertia are control capabilities of inverter-based resources; for MetroVolt they are design objectives. Real inertial emulation depends on available headroom and energy behind the inverter, tying back to the steady-burn and availability gates.

title: Synthetic Inertia From Power Electronics
lede: Inverters can emulate the stabilizing effect of spinning mass through control, a service that grows more valuable as physical inertia declines.
body: Physical inertia comes from the kinetic energy in spinning generators and resists sudden frequency change. Inverter-based resources have none by default, but their controls can measure the rate of frequency change and inject or absorb power to mimic an inertial response. This synthetic or virtual inertia can be delivered faster than a spinning machine because it is not limited by mechanical response.

The burner (MetroVolt), interfaced through power electronics, is a candidate for synthetic-inertia service. Its grid-forming inverter can be tuned to provide a defined inertial contribution to the local grid or microgrid it anchors.

Synthetic inertia requires an energy source behind the inverter to inject power in the first instants. That can come from the burner's output headroom, from a DC-link capacitor, or from a co-sited battery. Pairing with storage is often the practical way to deliver the fastest inertial response.

Synthetic inertia is a proven concept for inverter-based resources generally but unproven for MetroVolt specifically. Its magnitude depends on available energy headroom, which is constrained by the same steady-burn and availability gates discussed across this category.

title: Black-Start Capability
lede: Black-start is the ability to energize a dead grid without outside power; a grid-forming burner is a candidate black-start resource near load.
body: After a total blackout, the grid must be rebuilt from generators that can start without any external electricity. Most large plants cannot: they need station power to start. A black-start resource can energize itself and then bring a section of grid back to life, providing the voltage and frequency reference that other plants synchronize to.

A grid-forming, inverter-based burner is a natural black-start candidate provided it can start its own auxiliaries. The burner (MetroVolt), sited near load with grid-forming control, could energize a local network and anchor its restoration, a high-value service that is becoming scarcer as spinning black-start units retire.

What black-start requires of the burner

To black-start, the unit needs enough stored or on-site energy to bring the plasma and the direct-conversion train from cold to output, plus grid-forming inverters to set the initial reference and controls to manage inrush as loads are picked up in blocks. A co-sited battery can provide the initial station power to bootstrap the sequence.

Black-start is a design aspiration that depends on the machine starting reliably from cold, which is itself unproven given the plug-regime gate. It is a credible role for the architecture, verified only once the unit exists and its start-up sequence is demonstrated.

title: The Black-Start Sequence
lede: Restoring a grid proceeds in careful blocks; a near-load firm unit can serve as the anchor that energizes each step.
body: Bringing a grid back in blocks

Grid restoration is deliberate. A black-start unit first energizes a small, controlled section, called a cranking path, then picks up load in blocks, keeping generation and load balanced and voltage within limits at every step. Adding too much load at once trips the fragile restarting island. Larger plants are started along the path using power the black-start unit provides.

A near-load burner (MetroVolt) with grid-forming control can serve as the anchor for such a sequence in its local area, providing the reference voltage and frequency and the ramping capacity to pick up successive blocks of load.

Only a grid-forming source can set the reference that a restoring island needs. Grid-following inverters cannot start a dead grid because they require an existing reference. This is why the burner's inverter design intent includes grid-forming control.

The sequence above is standard grid-restoration practice; MetroVolt's ability to anchor it is a design objective contingent on reliable cold-start, which the plug-regime gate leaves open until the test program.

title: Islanding And Microgrids
lede: A firm generator can run a local network disconnected from the wider grid, keeping critical load powered through a wider outage.
body: Islanding is operating a local network, a campus, a district, a data center, disconnected from the main grid, supplied by local generation and storage. A microgrid is a network designed to do this intentionally: it can run connected to the grid or, when the grid fails, disconnect and keep its own load powered. Islanding requires a resource that can set voltage and frequency on its own.

A grid-forming burner (MetroVolt) sited at the load is well suited to anchor a microgrid. It supplies firm energy while inverter controls hold the island's voltage and frequency, and a co-sited battery covers the instant of disconnection and fast transients.

Why this matters for data centers and cities

A data center or a critical urban district that can island rides through wider grid disturbances without interruption. For compute loads that lose work on any outage, and for cities protecting critical services, the ability to island on a firm local source is a resilience asset distinct from raw energy supply.

Islanding is a design capability of a grid-forming firm unit. Its value for Tier III continuity is limited by the availability gate (0.86 to 0.995 vs 0.99982): a single islanded unit still needs redundancy and storage to approach data-center-grade continuity.

title: Campus Microgrid Integration
lede: On a data-center or city campus, a firm burner, storage, and controls form a microgrid that can run connected or islanded.
body: The campus as a controllable grid

A large campus, a data-center cluster, a university, a hospital district, is itself a small grid with its own generation, storage, and controllable loads. Integrating a firm burner into a campus microgrid means coordinating it with on-site batteries, renewables, and the grid connection so the campus can optimize for reliability and can island when the grid fails.

The burner (MetroVolt) is designed to be the firm anchor of such a campus. Sited behind or beside the meter, it supplies the sustained load while a battery handles fast transients and the microgrid controller arbitrates between the burner, storage, on-site solar, and the grid tie.

Connected, the campus can import or export and provide grid services. Islanded, it disconnects and runs on the burner and battery, keeping critical load powered. Transitioning smoothly between modes without dropping load is the central control challenge, and it favours grid-forming inverters and adequate storage.

Campus integration is a system-design story that presumes a working firm unit. The burner's contribution to continuity is bounded by the availability gate; the microgrid design uses redundancy and storage precisely to compensate for a single unit's 0.86 to 0.995 availability against a 0.99982 target.

title: Resilience Against Outages
lede: Resilience is the ability to keep critical load powered through disturbances; firm, sitable, islandable generation strengthens it.
body: Reliability is keeping the lights on during normal operation. Resilience is keeping critical load powered through and after severe events: storms, heat waves, equipment failures, or cyber-physical disruptions. Resilience depends on having generation close to load, the ability to island, and diverse, redundant supply that does not all fail together.

A near-demand burner (MetroVolt) contributes to resilience on several fronts: it sits at the load so it does not depend on long transmission that storms can sever; it can island a campus or district; and it can black-start local restoration. Its water independence also removes a failure mode, drought or intake loss, that constrains thermal plants.
