No single resource makes a grid resilient. A firm burner is one element among storage, renewables, and the wider grid. Its own availability gate means resilience plans must include redundancy rather than lean on one unit.

These resilience benefits are design intent enabled by siting, water independence, and inverter capabilities. They are realized only after the physics gates close and units are built and operated to demonstrate the capabilities.

title: Grid Resilience And Extreme Weather
lede: Extreme heat, cold, and storms stress supply and demand at once; firm, water-independent generation near load is a hedge against those events.
body: Extreme weather is dangerous because it raises demand and cuts supply simultaneously. A heat wave drives air-conditioning load while derating thermal plants and stressing cooling water. A deep cold snap raises heating load while freezing gas supply and equipment. Storms sever transmission. These correlated failures are what cause the largest blackouts.

A firm burner (MetroVolt) is designed to be robust to several of these mechanisms. It does not depend on cooling water, so heat waves and droughts do not derate it the way they derate steam plants. Sited near load, it is less exposed to transmission damage. Its fuel is stored on site, insulating it from fuel-delivery disruptions.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 210" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="210" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Illustrative availability under weather stress</text><text x="240" y="74" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Steam plant (heat wave derate)</text><rect x="250" y="56" width="238" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="496" y="74" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">70%</text><text x="240" y="114" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Gas plant (cold fuel risk)</text><rect x="250" y="96" width="204" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="462" y="114" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">60%</text><text x="240" y="154" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Water-light burner (target)</text><rect x="250" y="136" width="323" height="26" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="581" y="154" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">95%</text><text x="24" y="198" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Schematic; water independence reduces heat and drought derating.</text></svg>

No plant is fully weather-proof; extreme events can still damage any facility. And a single burner's baseline availability (0.86 to 0.995) is below what critical loads need, so weather resilience is realized through a redundant fleet and storage, not a lone unit.

Weather-resilience advantages follow from the water-light, near-load design and are compelling on paper. They remain design-stage claims until units are built and operated through real extreme events.

title: Drought And Water Resilience For Grids
lede: Thermal plants derate or shut when water runs short or warms; a water-light burner keeps firm output through droughts.
body: Water as a hidden reliability risk

Most firm generation, coal, gas, and fission, relies on water to reject heat. In drought, intake levels fall and discharge-temperature limits bind, forcing plants to derate or shut precisely when hot, dry conditions drive peak electricity demand. Water scarcity is therefore a grid-reliability risk, not only an environmental one.

The burner (MetroVolt) removes the steam cycle through direct energy conversion and so needs almost no cooling water. That makes its firm output largely independent of water availability, a resilience advantage in arid regions and during droughts when other firm plants are constrained.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="170" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Illustrative cooling-water dependence</text><text x="240" y="74" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Steam plant water need</text><rect x="250" y="56" width="340" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="598" y="74" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">100</text><text x="240" y="114" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Burner water need</text><rect x="250" y="96" width="17" height="26" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="275" y="114" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">5</text><text x="24" y="158" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">DEC removes the evaporative cooling draw; schematic.</text></svg>

Water independence also expands where firm capacity can be placed. Arid load pockets that cannot support a water-cooled plant can host a burner, adding firm capacity exactly where transmission and water are both stretched. This ties the water story to the grid-and-cities case.

Water resilience is one of the strongest and most concrete advantages of the DEC design, but it is still design-stage: the machine is low-neutron, not aneutronic, and final balance-of-plant water use will be fixed only when a unit is built. The advantage is directional and well grounded, not yet measured.

title: N-Minus-One Contingency Planning
lede: Grids are planned to survive the loss of any single element; firm capacity and redundancy are how that standard is met.
body: The N-1 criterion requires that a grid keep operating after the loss of any single major element, a generator, a line, or a transformer. Planners ensure enough spare firm capacity and network paths remain so that one failure does not cascade into a blackout. This drives reserve requirements and the value of redundancy.

A firm resource contributes to N-1 by being available to cover the loss of another element. But the resource itself is also an element that can fail, so its own outage must be survivable. This dual role is why fleet redundancy matters for the burner (MetroVolt).

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">N-1 contingency</text><rect x="55" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="113" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Element</text><text x="113" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">fails</text><line x1="171" y1="143" x2="187" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="187,138 193,143 187,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="193" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="251" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Reserves</text><text x="251" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">cover</text><line x1="309" y1="143" x2="325" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,138 331,143 325,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="389" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">System</text><text x="389" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">stays up</text><line x1="447" y1="143" x2="463" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="463,138 469,143 463,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="469" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="527" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">N-1</text><text x="527" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">met</text></svg>

Because a single MetroVolt unit has a design-stage availability of 0.86 to 0.995, planning around a single unit would violate N-1 for a critical load. A redundant set of units, or a unit plus grid tie and storage, satisfies the criterion: the loss of any one is covered by the others.

N-1 planning is standard grid practice and applies to any generator. For MetroVolt it is a reason the design leans on modular, redundant fleets rather than single large units, which also aligns with the availability gate.

title: The Availability Gate For Grid Service
lede: The design-stage availability of 0.86 to 0.995 trails the 0.99982 a hyperscale Tier III load expects; this is the load-bearing grid gate.
body: The number that governs the grid case

Of the four honest burner gates, availability bears most directly on grid and data-center service. The design-stage availability estimate for a burner unit is 0.86 to 0.995. A hyperscale Tier III data center is engineered for 0.99982. The difference is 30 to 100 times more downtime than the most demanding load will accept from a single source.

This does not defeat the case, but it defines it. A single burner (MetroVolt) is not, today, a sole Tier III source. It becomes suitable through redundancy, fleet operation, storage, and a grid tie, the same way any single generator is backed up in a high-reliability facility.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 210" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="210" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Availability (%)</text><text x="240" y="74" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Design low</text><rect x="250" y="56" width="292" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="550" y="74" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">86.0</text><text x="240" y="114" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Design high</text><rect x="250" y="96" width="338" height="26" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="596" y="114" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">99.5</text><text x="240" y="154" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Tier III</text><rect x="250" y="136" width="340" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="598" y="154" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">99.982</text><text x="24" y="198" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">0.86 to 0.995 estimated vs 0.99982 Tier III. Design-and-simulation finding.</text></svg>

At the design stage, availability is limited by unproven confinement (the plug regime is 166 to 830 times beyond experiment), by the maturity of the direct-conversion train, and by the absence of operating experience from which to estimate forced-outage rates. Each of these is a target of the test program rather than a settled figure.

The response is architectural: modular units, N-1 redundancy, co-sited storage to bridge trips, and retention of a grid connection. These raise effective availability above any single unit. The gate is stated plainly here because pretending otherwise would misrepresent a design-stage machine.
Design-and-simulation finding, not a built-hardware result.

title: Why Availability Matters For The Grid
lede: For firm service, being available at the moment of need is everything; a resource's grid value collapses if it is down when called.
body: Availability is the currency of firmness

A firm resource is only as good as its availability. Capacity that is out of service at the peak provides no reliability. This is why availability, not nameplate or average energy, sets a resource's capacity credit and its contribution to reserve margins and N-1 planning. For a data center pursuing near-perfect uptime, the sensitivity is extreme.

The burner (MetroVolt) is designed to be firm, but its design-stage single-unit availability (0.86 to 0.995) trails the 0.99982 that a Tier III load requires. Understanding why this matters explains the whole redundancy strategy in this category.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 258" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="258" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Value lost when a firm unit is unavailable</text><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="600" y2="200" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="60" y1="60" x2="60" y2="200" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="330" y="230" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">hour of day</text><text x="30" y="130" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39" transform="rotate(-90 30 130)">demand</text><path d="M60,110 C160,90 220,180 330,185 C440,180 520,80 600,70" fill="none" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M60,200 L60,150 L600,150 L600,200 Z" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.35"/><text x="500" y="175" font-size="11" fill="#232C39">firm generation</text><text x="360" y="95" font-size="11" fill="#232C39">net load</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">A firm resource contributes nothing during its own downtime.</text></svg>
From single unit to reliable service

Reliability engineering turns imperfect components into a reliable system through redundancy. Several units with independent failure modes, plus storage and a grid tie, deliver an effective availability far higher than any one unit. A data center already applies this principle to its own equipment; the burner fleet applies it to generation.

This page frames why the availability gate is load-bearing. It is not softened: a single MetroVolt unit is not a Tier III source today. The path to data-center-grade firmness runs through redundancy and the test program, not through a single machine.

title: Redundancy For Firmness
lede: Multiple units with independent failure modes deliver an effective reliability far above any single burner, which is how the availability gap is closed.
body: Turning imperfect units into firm service

No single generator is perfectly reliable. High-reliability systems achieve near-continuous service by combining several units so that the failure of one is covered by the others. If unit failures are independent, the probability that all fail at once is the product of their individual failure probabilities, which is far smaller than any one.

The burner (MetroVolt) is designed modular precisely to exploit this. A set of smaller units, plus co-sited storage to bridge the seconds after a trip and a grid tie as a further backstop, delivers an effective availability well above the 0.86 to 0.995 of a single unit, approaching what a critical load requires.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 210" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="210" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Illustrative effective availability (%)</text><text x="240" y="74" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">1 unit</text><rect x="250" y="56" width="323" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="581" y="74" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">95</text><text x="240" y="114" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">3 units (N-1)</text><rect x="250" y="96" width="337" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="595" y="114" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">99.0</text><text x="240" y="154" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">4 units + storage</text><rect x="250" y="136" width="340" height="26" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="598" y="154" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">99.9</text><text x="24" y="198" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Schematic; redundancy raises effective availability above any single unit.</text></svg>

Redundancy only helps if failures are independent. Shared fuel supply, shared controls, a common cooling fault, or a site-wide event can fail multiple units together (common mode). Good design separates these dependencies. Honest reliability accounting must not assume perfect independence.

Redundancy is the design answer to the availability gate, and it is sound engineering. But it presumes units that work; MetroVolt is design-stage, and per-unit availability is itself an estimate to be validated after the ~2032 test unit.

title: Reliability Through Redundant Fleets
lede: A fleet of modular units operated together provides continuous firm output even as individual units cycle through maintenance and forced outages.
body: For grid and data-center service, the meaningful unit of reliability is not a single machine but a fleet. With several units, one can be down for planned maintenance and another for a forced outage while the rest carry the load. Staggering maintenance and holding a reserve unit keeps firm output continuous.

The burner (MetroVolt) fleet is designed this way. Modularity lets capacity be matched to load and lets units be maintained without dropping the campus. This is the practical route to the continuity a Tier III data center needs, given that no single unit reaches 0.99982 availability.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 256" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="256" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">How a fleet stays firm</text><rect x="40" y="56" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="56" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="78" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Stagger planned maintenance so only one unit is down at a time</text><rect x="40" y="100" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="100" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="122" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Hold a reserve unit to cover forced outages</text><rect x="40" y="144" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="144" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="166" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Co-site storage to bridge the seconds after a trip</text><rect x="40" y="188" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="188" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="210" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Retain a grid tie as a final backstop</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Fleet-level reliability compensates for single-unit availability.</text></svg>

Larger fleets give higher effective availability, up to the point where common-mode failures dominate. Beyond that, adding units yields little, so the design must eliminate shared failure paths, especially in fuel supply, controls, and cooling.

Fleet reliability is a design strategy, and building a fleet raises a separate gate: helium-3 demand for a commercial unit is roughly 400 times domestic supply, so a large fleet depends on breeder-bred and lunar He-3. Fleet firmness and fuel supply are linked, and both are design-stage.

title: Maintenance And Scheduled Outages
lede: Planned maintenance is part of every plant's availability budget; scheduling it around a fleet keeps firm output continuous.
body: Availability is reduced by two kinds of downtime: planned outages for inspection, component replacement, and refuelling, and forced outages from unexpected faults. Planned outages can be scheduled for low-demand periods and staggered across a fleet; forced outages cannot. Both must fit within the availability budget a firm resource commits to.

The burner (MetroVolt) will require maintenance on its magnets, first wall, vacuum and cryogenic systems, and the direct-conversion train. Designing for accessibility and for module replacement shortens planned outages and improves availability.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Scheduling maintenance around a fleet</text><rect x="55" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="113" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Plan</text><text x="113" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">outage window</text><line x1="171" y1="143" x2="187" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="187,138 193,143 187,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="193" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="251" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Stagger</text><text x="251" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">across fleet</text><line x1="309" y1="143" x2="325" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,138 331,143 325,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="389" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Others</text><text x="389" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">carry load</text><line x1="447" y1="143" x2="463" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="463,138 469,143 463,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="469" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="527" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Firm</text><text x="527" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">maintained</text></svg>

Availability is won or lost in maintainability. Components arranged for quick access, modular sub-systems that can be swapped rather than repaired in place, and diagnostics that catch problems before they force an outage all reduce downtime. These are explicit design goals for the burner.

Maintenance intervals and durations for a burner are not yet known, because no unit has operated. The availability estimate of 0.86 to 0.995 already attempts to include planned and forced outages, but it is a design-stage figure to be refined once units run.

title: Modularity And Fleet Firmness
lede: Building firm capacity from modular units matches supply to load, enables redundancy, and supports phased near-demand deployment.
body: A modular design builds capacity from repeated units rather than one large plant. For grid and cities this brings several advantages: capacity can be added in increments that track demand growth, units provide the redundancy that firmness requires, and manufacturing repeated units builds experience that improves reliability over time.

The burner (MetroVolt) is conceived as modular units. A campus or a load pocket receives the number of units its load and reliability target require, with at least one spare for N-1. This is the same logic data centers apply to their own equipment, extended to generation.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 256" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="256" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">What modularity buys</text><rect x="40" y="56" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="56" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="78" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Match capacity to load and to demand growth</text><rect x="40" y="100" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="100" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="122" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Provide redundancy for N-1 firm service</text><rect x="40" y="144" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="144" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="166" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Phase construction on constrained urban sites</text><rect x="40" y="188" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="188" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="210" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Accumulate build experience to improve reliability</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Modularity underpins fleet-level firmness.</text></svg>

Reaching fleet scale is a manufacturing and supply-chain problem as much as a physics one. The design path runs from a first test unit around 2032 to commercial units around 2036 and onward to fleets, with reliability improving as units accumulate.

Fleet firmness depends on both building many units and fuelling them. The helium-3 supply gate, roughly 400 times domestic supply per commercial unit, means fleet scale is contingent on breeder-bred and lunar He-3. Modularity is a design strength; fuel is the constraint on how far it can scale.

title: From Two To Many Firm Units
lede: Scaling from a test unit to a firm fleet is a manufacturing and supply problem layered on top of the open physics gates.
body: A single working unit is a physics demonstration; a firm grid resource is a fleet. Getting from one to many requires repeatable manufacturing, a qualified supply chain for high-field magnets and direct-conversion hardware, and enough fuel to run every unit continuously. Each of these is a distinct program beyond the first machine.

The burner (MetroVolt) roadmap moves from a test unit around 2032 to commercial units around 2036 and then to fleets that provide firm capacity at grid scale. Reliability is expected to improve as units accumulate operating hours and as manufacturing matures.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Scale-up roadmap</text><rect x="55" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="113" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Test unit</text><text x="113" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">~2032</text><line x1="171" y1="143" x2="187" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="187,138 193,143 187,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="193" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="251" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Commercial</text><text x="251" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">~2036</text><line x1="309" y1="143" x2="325" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,138 331,143 325,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="389" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Fleet</text><text x="389" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">grid scale</text><line x1="447" y1="143" x2="463" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="463,138 469,143 463,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="469" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="527" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Firm</text><text x="527" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">at scale</text></svg>
What must be true to scale

Fleet scale requires that the physics gates close on the test unit, that manufacturing can produce 26.49 T plug magnets and DEC trains repeatably, and that fuel exists. The last is the binding external constraint: He-3 demand at commercial scale is roughly 400 times domestic supply, which is why the breeder-bred and lunar He-3 pathways are part of the plan.
The scale-up is a plan, not an achievement. It is sequenced deliberately behind the breeder build and the test unit, and every step is contingent on the prior one. No firm fleet exists today.

title: Co-Location With Load Centers
lede: Placing a firm burner at the load, behind or beside the meter, delivers power without crossing the grid and adds local resilience.
body: Co-location means siting generation at the point of consumption: a burner beside a data-center campus, a city district, or an industrial cluster. Power delivered at the load avoids transmission losses, congestion, and the interconnection burden of exporting across the system. It also gives the load a local firm source it can island onto.

The burner (MetroVolt) is designed for co-location because it is water-light and compact, so it can sit where thermal plants cannot. For a data center, this means firm power at the fence line rather than contracted from distant plants over congested wires.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 258" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="258" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Co-located firm generation</text><rect x="360" y="90" width="220" height="120" rx="8" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="470" y="80" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Load center</text><rect x="375" y="150" width="26" height="60" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="415" y="120" width="26" height="90" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="455" y="160" width="26" height="50" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="495" y="130" width="26" height="80" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="535" y="145" width="26" height="65" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="70" y="120" width="150" height="70" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="70" y="120" width="150" height="8" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="145" y="150" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">MetroVolt</text><text x="145" y="168" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">unit</text><line x1="220" y1="155" x2="360" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="3"/><text x="290" y="140" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">short interconnect</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">A burner at the fence line delivers firm power without crossing the grid.</text></svg>

Co-location can be behind the customer's meter, primarily serving on-site load with the grid as backup, or beside it as a front-of-meter generator that also exports. The choice affects interconnection scope, grid-service participation, and how stand-by charges apply. Both keep generation close to the load.

Co-location is a siting advantage, not a physics claim. The unit still faces all four gates, and its availability (0.86 to 0.995) means a co-located data center still needs redundant units, storage, and a grid tie to reach Tier III continuity. Proximity helps resilience; it does not replace redundancy.
related: Relieving The Grid For Data Centers

title: Behind The Meter Versus Front Of Meter
lede: Whether a co-sited burner serves a customer directly or connects as a grid generator changes its interconnection, services, and backup role.
body: Behind the meter generation sits on the customer's side and primarily serves that customer's load, drawing from the grid only when needed. Front of the meter generation connects as a grid resource that can serve any load and export, participating in wholesale markets and grid services. The same physical burner can be configured either way.

For a data center, a behind-the-meter burner (MetroVolt) supplies the campus directly, with the grid as backup, reducing interconnection scope. A front-of-meter unit exports and provides grid services but faces fuller interconnection and market obligations.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 256" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="256" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Behind vs front of meter</text><rect x="40" y="56" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="56" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="78" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Behind: serves the host load, grid as backup, lighter interconnect</text><rect x="40" y="100" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="100" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="122" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Front: exports to the grid, provides ancillary services</text><rect x="40" y="144" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="144" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="166" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Behind: simpler queue, limited market participation</text><rect x="40" y="188" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="188" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="210" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Front: full grid-code and market obligations</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">The same unit can be configured either way.</text></svg>

A behind-the-meter unit still typically keeps a grid connection for backup and for the times its own units are in maintenance, which brings stand-by considerations. This grid tie is also part of how the availability gate is managed: the grid backstops the on-site fleet.

The choice is a project and regulatory decision that presumes a working unit. MetroVolt's configuration is not fixed at the design stage; both models are enabled by the power-electronics interface and near-demand siting.

title: Relieving The Grid For Data Centers
lede: Data-center clusters overwhelm local grids faster than new lines can be built; a co-sited firm burner serves the load without loading the grid.
body: A load growing faster than the grid

AI and cloud campuses now request hundreds of megawatts at single sites, and clusters of them appear faster than transmission can be planned and built. The result is interconnection backlogs, congestion, and communities where a new campus competes with existing users for grid capacity and, if the power is thermal, for water.

A co-sited burner (MetroVolt) serves the campus load locally, so that demand does not have to be carried across the grid at all. This relieves the surrounding system, freeing grid capacity for other users and deferring transmission that would otherwise be needed to import power to the campus.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 258" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="258" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Serving the campus, sparing the grid</text><rect x="360" y="90" width="220" height="120" rx="8" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="470" y="80" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Load center</text><rect x="375" y="150" width="26" height="60" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="415" y="120" width="26" height="90" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="455" y="160" width="26" height="50" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="495" y="130" width="26" height="80" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="535" y="145" width="26" height="65" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="70" y="120" width="150" height="70" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="70" y="120" width="150" height="8" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="145" y="150" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">MetroVolt</text><text x="145" y="168" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">unit</text><line x1="220" y1="155" x2="360" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="3"/><text x="290" y="140" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">short interconnect</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">On-site firm power means the campus load never crosses the wider grid.</text></svg>

Because direct energy conversion removes the steam cycle, a co-sited burner also spares local water. A campus that would otherwise draw thermal power, and its off-site evaporative water footprint, from a stressed grid instead runs on a water-light local source. Grid relief and water relief come together.

This is the central grid-and-cities argument for MetroVolt, and it is design-stage. The availability gate is decisive here: a data center demands 0.99982 uptime, far above a single unit's 0.86 to 0.995, so on-site generation must be a redundant fleet with storage and a grid tie, not one machine.

title: District Heat And Waste Heat To Cities
lede: The neutron-driven and residual heat a burner produces can serve district heating, using near-load siting to deliver warmth as well as power.
body: Heat is a resource, not only a loss

Direct energy conversion turns most of the charged-particle power into electricity, but a burner still produces heat: 5.44 percent of fusion power is carried by neutrons, and there are residual thermal losses in the machine and power electronics. In a plant far from people this heat is rejected. Sited near a city, it can instead serve district heating.

District heating distributes hot water through a network to warm buildings. A near-demand burner (MetroVolt) could supply this heat as a by-product of firm electricity, improving overall energy use in cold-climate cities where heating demand is large.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Waste heat to district heating</text><rect x="55" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="113" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Neutron +</text><text x="113" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">residual heat</text><line x1="171" y1="143" x2="187" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="187,138 193,143 187,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="193" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="251" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Heat</text><text x="251" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">recovery</text><line x1="309" y1="143" x2="325" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,138 331,143 325,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="389" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">District</text><text x="389" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">network</text><line x1="447" y1="143" x2="463" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="463,138 469,143 463,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="469" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="527" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">City</text><text x="527" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">heating</text></svg>

Delivering both electricity and useful heat is combined heat and power (CHP). It raises the fraction of fuel energy put to use. For MetroVolt, the electricity is primary and comes from DEC; the heat is a secondary output that near-load siting makes usable rather than wasted.

District heat is an opportunity that depends on siting near a heat network and on the plant's residual heat being at a useful temperature. It is a secondary benefit, not a driver, and like everything here it is design-stage. It does not change the water story: DEC still removes the large evaporative cooling draw.

title: Combined Heat And Power For Cities
lede: A near-demand burner can deliver firm electricity and useful heat together, raising energy utilization where both are needed.
body: Combined heat and power (CHP) plants deliver electricity and capture heat that would otherwise be rejected, supplying it to nearby buildings or industry. CHP only works when the plant is close to a heat demand, because heat cannot travel far. That makes CHP a natural fit for near-city and urban-edge siting.

The burner (MetroVolt) is primarily a firm electricity source through direct energy conversion, but its residual and neutron-driven heat can be recovered for district heating or industrial process heat where a plant is sited near such demand. This adds value without changing the electrical output.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">CHP for near-demand siting</text><rect x="55" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="113" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Burner</text><text x="113" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">firm power</text><line x1="171" y1="143" x2="187" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="187,138 193,143 187,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="193" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="251" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Recover</text><text x="251" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">residual heat</text><line x1="309" y1="143" x2="325" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,138 331,143 325,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="389" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Deliver</text><text x="389" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">heat + power</text><line x1="447" y1="143" x2="463" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="463,138 469,143 463,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="469" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="527" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">City +</text><text x="527" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">industry</text></svg>

CHP is valuable where there is a steady, co-located heat demand: a cold-climate city district, an industrial cluster, or a data center that can use warm water. Without a nearby heat sink the heat is simply rejected, which the water-light design does with minimal water anyway.

CHP is a siting-dependent secondary benefit at the design stage. It presumes a working unit, a nearby heat demand, and heat-recovery equipment. It complements, and does not replace, the firm-power and water-light arguments that drive the grid-and-cities case.

title: Water-Light Siting In Cities
lede: Because direct energy conversion removes the steam cycle, a burner can be sited in water-constrained cities where thermal plants cannot.
body: Water is the usual siting blocker

The reason large firm plants sit far from cities is often water: they need a river, lake, or coastline to reject heat. Cities and arid regions rarely have spare water for a thermal plant, so firm capacity is imported over long lines. Removing the water need removes that blocker and opens urban and arid sites to firm generation.

The burner (MetroVolt) rejects almost no heat to water because direct energy conversion replaces the steam cycle. Its cooling needs are small, met with closed-loop or dry cooling, so it can be sited where water is scarce, exactly where firm capacity and transmission are most constrained.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="170" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Illustrative cooling-water dependence</text><text x="240" y="74" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Steam plant water need</text><rect x="250" y="56" width="340" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="598" y="74" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">100</text><text x="240" y="114" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Burner water need</text><rect x="250" y="96" width="17" height="26" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="275" y="114" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">5</text><text x="24" y="158" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Water independence is what enables urban and arid siting; schematic.</text></svg>

Water-light siting lets firm capacity be placed at the load in cities and arid load pockets, which relieves transmission and adds local resilience. This is where the water story and the grid-and-cities story converge: the same property that answers the data-center water crisis also enables near-demand siting.

The water-light property is one of the most concrete design advantages, but the machine is low-neutron, not aneutronic, and final water use is fixed only when built. Urban siting also still requires a nuclear safety case, licensing, and community consent.

title: Siting In Arid Load Pockets
lede: Arid regions with growing demand cannot host water-cooled plants; a water-light burner can add firm capacity exactly where it is scarcest.
body: Where firm capacity is hardest to add

Fast-growing arid regions face a compounding problem: demand rises, but there is neither water for thermal plants nor easy transmission to import firm power. Solar is abundant but variable, so firmness is scarce. These arid load pockets are where a water-independent firm resource has the most to offer.

The burner (MetroVolt) needs almost no cooling water, so it can be sited in an arid load pocket to add firm, dispatchable capacity that firms the local solar and relieves the transmission that would otherwise import power. It does this without competing with communities for scarce water.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 258" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="258" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Firm capacity in an arid pocket</text><rect x="360" y="90" width="220" height="120" rx="8" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="470" y="80" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Load center</text><rect x="375" y="150" width="26" height="60" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="415" y="120" width="26" height="90" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="455" y="160" width="26" height="50" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="495" y="130" width="26" height="80" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="535" y="145" width="26" height="65" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.8"/><rect x="70" y="120" width="150" height="70" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="70" y="120" width="150" height="8" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="145" y="150" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">MetroVolt</text><text x="145" y="168" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">unit</text><line x1="220" y1="155" x2="360" y2="150" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="3"/><text x="290" y="140" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">short interconnect</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">A water-light burner firms local solar without drawing scarce water.</text></svg>

In drought-prone regions, water-cooled firm plants derate when they are needed most, during hot, dry peaks. A water-light burner keeps firm output through those conditions, making it a resilience asset as well as a firming resource in arid grids.

Arid-siting advantage follows directly from the DEC water story and is well grounded. It remains design-stage, and the availability gate still applies: even in an arid pocket, data-center-grade firmness needs a redundant fleet, not a single unit.

title: Permitting And Community Siting
lede: Siting a burner near people requires a nuclear safety case, licensing, and community consent, on the critical path alongside the physics.
body: Near-load siting has non-technical gates too

The advantages that let a burner sit near a city, water independence and a compact footprint, do not remove the need for a nuclear safety case, a licence, emergency planning, and the consent of the community that will host it. For any urban-adjacent nuclear facility these are as decisive as the engineering, and they take time.

The burner (MetroVolt) is low-neutron, not aneutronic: 5.44 percent of fusion power is in neutrons, so there is activation and shielding to account for, and activated-material handling over the plant's life. The safety case addresses these honestly rather than claiming a hazard-free machine.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 256" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="256" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Non-technical siting requirements</text><rect x="40" y="56" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="56" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="78" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Nuclear safety case and licensing</text><rect x="40" y="100" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="100" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="122" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Emergency planning appropriate to a near-load site</text><rect x="40" y="144" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="144" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="166" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Community engagement and consent</text><rect x="40" y="188" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="188" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="210" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Zoning, land use, and local permitting</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">On the critical path alongside the physics gates.</text></svg>

Community acceptance is easier to earn for a plant that is transparent about its heat and material handling, needs little water, and brings local resilience and possibly district heat. But acceptance must be earned per site, not assumed from the technology's merits.

Licensing and consent are real constraints independent of the physics gates and are part of why the commercial timeline is around 2036. The water and footprint advantages help the case; they do not shortcut it.

title: The Grid Services A Burner Can Offer
lede: Beyond energy, a firm inverter-based burner can supply capacity, reserves, voltage support, frequency response, and black-start.
body: A grid buys several distinct products. Energy is the bulk product. Capacity is the promise to be available at the peak. Ancillary services keep the system stable moment to moment: reserves, frequency response, reactive-power and voltage support, and black-start. A resource that can supply many of these is more valuable than one that supplies energy alone.

The burner (MetroVolt), firm and inverter-based, is designed to offer a broad portfolio: firm energy and capacity from its steady-state core, and a range of ancillary services from its power-electronics interface.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="300" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Portfolio of grid services</text><rect x="40" y="56" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="56" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="78" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Energy and firm capacity from steady-state operation</text><rect x="40" y="100" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="100" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="122" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Operating reserves and load following</text><rect x="40" y="144" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="144" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="166" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Frequency response and synthetic inertia</text><rect x="40" y="188" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="188" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="210" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Reactive power and local voltage support</text><rect x="40" y="232" width="560" height="34" rx="6" fill="#232C39"/><rect x="40" y="232" width="6" height="34" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="58" y="254" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="#fff">Black-start and islanding for local resilience</text><text x="24" y="290" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Enabled by steady-state core plus inverter interface.</text></svg>

Providing several services from one asset improves its usefulness to the grid and the load it serves, and lets a co-sited fleet cover more of a campus's needs. It is also why near-demand siting is attractive: many of these services, voltage support, black-start, islanding, are most valuable delivered locally.

This portfolio is a design capability set, credible for a firm inverter-based resource but unproven for MetroVolt. Each service also depends on the unit being available, tying the whole portfolio back to the availability gate.

title: Ancillary Services: An Overview
lede: Ancillary services keep the grid stable between the bulk energy transactions; firm, flexible resources are well placed to supply them.
body: The services that keep the grid stable

Ancillary services are the supporting products that maintain grid reliability moment to moment: regulation and reserves to balance supply and demand on short timescales, frequency response to arrest disturbances, reactive power to hold voltage, and black-start to recover from a blackout. They are procured separately from energy and are increasingly scarce as spinning plants retire.

The burner (MetroVolt) can supply many of these because it is firm, dispatchable, and inverter-based. Fast, programmable control of active and reactive power lets it provide regulation, reserves, and voltage support; grid-forming control enables frequency response and black-start.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Categories of ancillary services</text><rect x="55" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="113" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Regulation</text><text x="113" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">reserves</text><line x1="171" y1="143" x2="187" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="187,138 193,143 187,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="193" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="251" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Frequency</text><text x="251" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">response</text><line x1="309" y1="143" x2="325" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,138 331,143 325,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="389" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Voltage</text><text x="389" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">support</text><line x1="447" y1="143" x2="463" y2="143" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="463,138 469,143 463,148" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="469" y="110" width="116" height="66" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="527" y="138" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Black</text><text x="527" y="156" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">start</text></svg>

Several ancillary services are most useful delivered near where they are needed. Voltage support helps the local pocket; black-start and islanding protect the local network. A near-demand burner is therefore well placed to supply the services a growing load center most needs.

Ancillary-service capability follows from the inverter interface and steady-state core, but for MetroVolt it is a design objective. Each service requires the unit to be online and stable, which returns to the availability and plug-regime gates.

title: Ramp Rate And Dispatch Demonstration
lede: How fast a firm unit can change output is a key dispatch parameter; for the burner it is set by plasma control and remains to be demonstrated.
body: Ramp rate as a dispatch parameter

A dispatchable resource is characterized partly by its ramp rate: how many megawatts per minute it can add or shed. High ramp rates let a unit follow the steep evening net-load neck and cover sudden losses of other generation. Steam plants ramp slowly because of thermal inertia; a burner without a steam cycle is not bound by that limit.

In the burner (MetroVolt), output is changed by adjusting fuelling, heating, and the direct-conversion bias, and the electrical path has little thermal mass. The ramp is therefore limited by how fast plasma parameters can be moved while holding confinement, not by boiler metal.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 258" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="258" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Following a steep ramp</text><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="600" y2="200" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="60" y1="60" x2="60" y2="200" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="330" y="230" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">hour of day</text><text x="30" y="130" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39" transform="rotate(-90 30 130)">demand</text><path d="M60,110 C160,90 220,180 330,185 C440,180 520,80 600,70" fill="none" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M60,200 L60,150 L600,150 L600,200 Z" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.35"/><text x="500" y="175" font-size="11" fill="#232C39">firm generation</text><text x="360" y="95" font-size="11" fill="#232C39">net load</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Ramp is set by plasma control, not by steam-cycle thermal inertia.</text></svg>

A dispatch demonstration must establish the stable operating band, the achievable ramp rate within it, and that repeated ramping does not degrade confinement or hardware. These are precisely the parameters the ~2032 test unit is meant to measure.

No ramp rate has been demonstrated. The plug operating regime is 166 to 830 times beyond any device, so the true dispatch band and ramp are unknown today. DEC removes the thermal-inertia limit in principle; whether the plasma tolerates fast dispatch is an open question for the test program.

title: Firm Capacity For Electrification
lede: Electrifying transport, heating, and industry raises and reshapes demand; firm, sitable capacity is needed to serve the new peaks.
body: As transport, building heat, and industrial processes electrify, total electricity demand rises and its shape changes. Winter heating peaks grow where electric heat pumps replace gas; vehicle charging adds evening load. These new peaks must be met with firm capacity, not only more average energy, and often in the same congested urban areas where the loads sit.

The burner (MetroVolt) is designed to add firm, dispatchable capacity near these growing loads. Its water independence and compact footprint let it be placed in the cities and regions where electrified demand concentrates and where transmission is already stretched.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 258" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="258" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">A taller, sharper electrified peak</text><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="600" y2="200" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="60" y1="60" x2="60" y2="200" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="330" y="230" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">hour of day</text><text x="30" y="130" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39" transform="rotate(-90 30 130)">demand</text><path d="M60,110 C160,90 220,180 330,185 C440,180 520,80 600,70" fill="none" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="2.5"/><path d="M60,200 L60,150 L600,150 L600,200 Z" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.35"/><text x="500" y="175" font-size="11" fill="#232C39">firm generation</text><text x="360" y="95" font-size="11" fill="#232C39">net load</text><text x="24" y="246" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Electrification raises peaks that firm, near-load capacity must serve.</text></svg>

Electric heating shifts many grids toward a winter-evening peak that coincides with low solar and often low wind. This is exactly the multi-day, weather-correlated stress that firm generation, not storage alone, is needed to cover. A firm burner is designed for this role.

Firm capacity for electrification is a role the architecture suits, contingent on the physics gates and on fleet-scale fuel supply. The commercial timeline is around 2036, so this is a contribution to later phases of electrification, not to near-term peaks.

title: Peak Demand And Heat Waves
lede: Peaks driven by heat or cold stress supply and demand together; water-independent firm generation is a hedge against those correlated stresses.
body: When demand peaks and supply weakens

The tightest grid hours often come during heat waves and cold snaps, when demand spikes for cooling or heating just as supply is constrained. In heat, thermal plants derate as cooling water warms and air-cooling loses effectiveness; in cold, fuel supplies and equipment can freeze. Firm capacity that is robust to these conditions is what prevents shortfalls.

The burner (MetroVolt), being water-independent, does not derate when cooling water warms or runs short, so it holds firm output through heat waves better than a water-cooled thermal plant. Sited near load, it is also less exposed to the transmission stress that peaks bring.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 210" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="210" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Illustrative firm output during a heat wave</text><text x="240" y="74" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Water-cooled plant in heat</text><rect x="250" y="56" width="238" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="496" y="74" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">70%</text><text x="240" y="114" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Air-cooled plant in heat</text><rect x="250" y="96" width="272" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="530" y="114" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">80%</text><text x="240" y="154" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Water-light burner (target)</text><rect x="250" y="136" width="323" height="26" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="581" y="154" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">95%</text><text x="24" y="198" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Schematic; water independence reduces heat-wave derating.</text></svg>

Heat-wave and cold-snap risks are correlated across a region: many plants derate at once, and demand peaks everywhere together. A firm resource that resists these mechanisms adds value precisely because it is not correlated with the common failure mode.

The heat-wave advantage is grounded in the water-light design, but it is design-stage, and single-unit availability (0.86 to 0.995) still requires fleet redundancy to deliver dependable peak coverage.

title: The Helium-3 Supply Gate And Fleet Firmness
lede: A commercial burner needs roughly 400 times the domestic helium-3 supply; fleet-scale firm power depends on fuel that does not yet exist terrestrially.
body: The fuel that firmness depends on

A D-3He burner runs on helium-3, which is extremely scarce on Earth. The design-stage estimate is that a single commercial unit would demand roughly 400 times the entire domestic helium-3 supply. Firm power at fleet scale therefore depends on a fuel supply that does not exist at terrestrial scale today. This is the third honest gate.

This is why the program is sequenced as it is. The breeder (Hyperion) is built first and, among its products, breeds helium-3 (about 1.97 kg/yr class alongside its tritium). Beyond that, lunar helium-3 is the long-term source. The burner fleet's firmness is gated on these pathways maturing.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="170" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Illustrative He-3 demand vs supply (ratio)</text><text x="240" y="74" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Domestic He-3 supply</text><rect x="250" y="56" width="1" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="259" y="74" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">1x</text><text x="240" y="114" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">One commercial unit demand</text><rect x="250" y="96" width="340" height="26" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="598" y="114" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">400x</text><text x="24" y="158" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">~400x domestic supply per commercial unit. Design-and-simulation finding.</text></svg>
Why it bears on the grid case

Everything in this category, firming renewables, multi-day lulls, resource adequacy, relieving data-center load, presumes not one unit but a fleet running continuously. Continuous fleet operation is exactly what the fuel gate constrains. Fleet firmness and fuel supply cannot be separated.

This gate is stated plainly and not softened. It is a physics-and-supply fact, not an economic one. It is the reason the breeder comes first and why lunar helium-3 is part of the long-term plan. Until the fuel pathway scales, fleet-scale firm power is a design goal, not an available service.

title: Plug Stress And Regime Gates For The Grid Case
lede: Two physics gates, plug-coil stress and an operating regime far beyond experiment, underlie whether the burner can deliver firm power at all.
body: The gates beneath the grid promises

Every grid capability in this category, firmness, dispatch, ramp, black-start, presumes the burner sustains a D-3He burn. Two of the four honest gates concern exactly that. First, the plug coil is overstressed roughly 3 to 3.9 times at the design bore, so as specified it is not yet buildable. Second, the plug operating regime sits 166 to 830 times beyond any device operated to date, so its behaviour cannot be post-dicted from existing data.

The burner (MetroVolt) design uses a 26.49 T plug and 17 T throat to set up the confining potential. These are the fields the plug coil must withstand, and the regime figure reflects how far past demonstrated operation that confinement lies.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 210" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="210" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Plug and regime gates (illustrative scale)</text><text x="240" y="74" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Plug coil stress (x limit)</text><rect x="250" y="56" width="2" height="26" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="260" y="74" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">3.9x</text><text x="240" y="114" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Regime beyond device (x, low)</text><rect x="250" y="96" width="68" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="326" y="114" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">166x</text><text x="240" y="154" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="#232C39">Regime beyond device (x, high)</text><rect x="250" y="136" width="340" height="26" rx="3" fill="#232C39"/><text x="598" y="154" font-size="11.5" fill="#232C39">830x</text><text x="24" y="198" font-size="11" fill="#232C39" opacity="0.7">Stress ~3-3.9x; regime 166-830x beyond any device. Design-and-simulation findings.</text></svg>
Why they come before the grid case

If the plug cannot be built as specified, or the regime cannot be reached and held, there is no firm output to dispatch. These gates are logically upstream of every grid capability described here. Stating them plainly is what keeps the grid case honest.

Closing these gates is the purpose of the design-and-simulation work now and of the ~2032 test unit. Magnet engineering must reach the required fields at acceptable stress, and experiments must probe the regime. Until then, the firm-power promises here are conditional on this physics.
Design-and-simulation finding, not a built-hardware result.

title: The Grid Of 2036: A Design-Stage Scenario
lede: A commercial burner is targeted around 2036; this page sketches the grid role it is designed for, and what must be true first.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) begins construction in Q2 2027 with first-of-a-kind first tritium around 2030. A burner test unit follows around 2032, and a commercial burner around 2036. Only after that can a firm burner fleet begin to contribute to the grid. Everything in this category describes the role such a fleet is designed to play from the later 2030s onward.

In that scenario, water-light burners (MetroVolt) sit near data-center clusters and cities, firming renewable-heavy grids, relieving transmission, and providing local resilience, while the breeder-bred and lunar helium-3 pathways supply their fuel.

This scenario is contingent on all four gates closing: the plug coil buildable at 26.49 T without 3-3.9x overstress, the operating regime reached and held despite being 166-830x beyond experiment, helium-3 available at roughly 400x today's supply through breeding and lunar sources, and availability improved from 0.86-0.995 toward what critical loads need, via redundant fleets.

This is a design-stage scenario, not a forecast. No burner has produced net power. The value of stating the scenario is to make the sequence and its conditions explicit, so the grid role is understood as a goal with named prerequisites rather than a promise.

title: Honest Grid Readiness Summary
lede: A single-page accounting of where the burner stands as a grid resource today: strong design fit, four open physics gates, all design-stage.
body: What is designed and what is proven

The burner (MetroVolt) is designed to be an excellent firm, dispatchable, near-load grid resource: steady-state D-3He core, direct energy conversion with little thermal inertia, near-zero water so it can sit in cities and arid pockets, and an inverter interface that can offer a broad grid-services portfolio. None of this is yet proven on hardware. The machine is at the design-and-simulation stage.

The frozen design point is clear: 85.0 MW-class breeder physics anchors the program, while the burner runs at a 26.49 T plug and 17 T throat with a 5.44 percent neutron fraction (low-neutron, not aneutronic) and direct conversion. These numbers are fixed; the grid capabilities built on them are targets.

The responses are architectural and sequenced: breeder first for helium-3 and to prove the program; a ~2032 test unit to probe the plug and regime; modular, redundant fleets plus storage and a grid tie to close the availability gap; and lunar helium-3 for long-term fuel. Each response is a plan, not a result.

As a grid resource, the burner is a strong design fit for the problems grids and cities face, and honest about four open gates that stand between the design and firm power. The right reading is a promising, unproven architecture with a clear, gated path, targeted commercial around 2036.
